title: The Tent and the Culvert: the Colonel, the Green Book, and Forty-Two Years of the State of the Masses
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Tent at Qasr Abu Hadi

stops.name: Qasr Abu Hadi, birth in the tent
stops.date_confidence: disputed. Wikipedia gives c. 1942; Simple Wikipedia and many obituaries give 7 June 1943. No birth record exists for a herding family in the district, and the day and month are the conventional ones rather than documented ones.
stops.campa: In a goat-hair tent in the Qadhadhfa tribal district south of Sirte, a herding family of Italian Libya has a son. His father cannot read. His paternal grandfather, the family holds, was killed fighting the Italian invasion of 1911, the year Gabriele D'Annunzio wrote crusading verse for that invasion from exile at Arcachon and Benito Mussolini built a socialist reputation in Milan denouncing it. The boy walks in to primary school at Sirte, the only pupil in the room without a fixed house, and sleeps back in the tent.
suggested_refs: The Qadhadhfa district at Qasr Abu Hadi, outside Sirte, birth country of the Free Officers' leader
sources: Blundy and Lycett, Qaddafi and the Libyan Revolution (1987)

stops.name: Sabha, the schoolboy's demonstration
stops.date_confidence: October 1961 attested; the day of the demonstration is not recorded in the sources reached, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: At the preparatory school in the Fezzan oasis he reads Nasser and runs a clandestine pan-Arabist cell among the boarders. When Syria secedes from the United Arab Republic he organizes a street demonstration against the breakup. He is arrested with his companions and expelled, and the expulsion is served on the whole family: they are put out of Sabha. He is eighteen or nineteen. The household loads what it has and goes five hundred kilometres north to the coast, where he finishes his schooling.
suggested_refs: Sabha Preparatory School in the Fezzan, seedbed of the officers' cell
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

stops.name: Misrata, the school on the coast
stops.date_confidence: the Misrata schooling is dated 1961-1963; the month of arrival is not recorded, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He finishes secondary school on the coast at Misrata, and here the network that will take the country is assembled: fellow pupils and, soon, fellow cadets, sworn to Nasser's example and to the removal of King Idris. The organization takes the name the Free Officers Movement, copied outright from the Egyptian original that made Nasser. Fifty years later this same coastal town will keep his body in a commercial freezer and let the public file past it for four days.
suggested_refs: The secondary school at Misrata, where the Free Officers Movement was first assembled
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

stops.name: Benghazi, the Royal Military Academy
stops.date_confidence: enrolment 1963, graduation 1965 attested; month of entry unrecorded, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: He enters the Royal Military Academy in the Cyrenaican capital and graduates in 1965 a signals officer, recruiting the core of the conspiracy among his fellow cadets. Signals is the correct trade for what he intends: whoever holds the transmitters holds the announcement. The academy trains the sons of a province Italy spent two decades pacifying by air and internment camp; the cadets in this classroom are the grandsons of the men that campaign was fought against, and the king they will overthrow inherited the settlement it left behind.
suggested_refs: The Royal Military Academy of Benghazi, graduating class of 1965

stops.name: Beaconsfield, the course in the imperial country
stops.date_confidence: 1966 attested for training in the United Kingdom; month unrecorded, defaulted. The location is contested: Wikipedia's Gaddafi article names no British site at all, and the Beaconsfield establishment was the Army School of Education, with signals instruction given at Bovington Camp in Dorset. The pin follows Beaconsfield and the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The Libyan army sends a group of young officers to Britain for further training and he is among them. At Beaconsfield he is put through an English-language course at the Army School of Education; the signals instruction is given at Bovington Camp in Dorset. He is the subject of a kingdom that keeps British and American bases on its soil, learning the trade of transmission in the country that garrisons it. Four years after he comes home, both sets of bases are closed by his order.
suggested_refs: The Army School of Education at Beaconsfield and the signals school at Bovington Camp

stops.name: Benghazi, the Berka barracks seized
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Operation Jerusalem opens before dawn. He takes the Berka barracks in Benghazi himself while Umar Muhayshi seizes the Tripoli barracks and Abdessalam Jalloud takes the capital's anti-aircraft batteries; airports, police depots and radio stations fall in both cities in a few hours. King Idris is abroad taking a cure in Turkey. No fighting is recorded. He is twenty-seven, a signals captain, and by breakfast the ranking authority in an oil state of two million people.
stops.quote: Revolution is when the masses make the revolution. A people's revolution.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Oriana Fallaci, Corriere della Sera, 2 December 1979, cited via Wikiquote's sourced entry
suggested_refs: The Berka barracks at Benghazi, first objective of the 1969 revolution
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

stops.name: Tripoli, the Libyan Arab Republic proclaimed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The radio announces the end of the monarchy and the birth of the Libyan Arab Republic. A Revolutionary Command Council of officers is named and he chairs it. He promotes himself colonel and will take no higher rank for forty-two years. He refuses general's stars, and he refuses the presidency and every other office that carries a legal definition. The state has no constitution and no parliament. It has a council, a colonel, and the largest proven oil reserves in Africa.
suggested_refs: The Tripoli radio station, from which the fall of the monarchy was announced
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

stops.name: Tripoli, the foreign bases close and the Italians go
stops.date_confidence: base withdrawals attested to 1970; the expropriation and expulsion attested to October 1970. The 7 October date is the day later kept as a national holiday and is not separately confirmed in the pool.
stops.campa: Within a year the British evacuate their garrisons and the Americans give up Wheelus, the largest United States air base outside the continental states. In October the government expropriates Italian-owned property and expels the roughly twelve thousand Italian settlers along with the remaining Libyan Jews. The colonial account, opened by the invasion that killed his grandfather, is declared closed by decree. Thirty-eight years later Italy will reopen it in Benghazi and pay five billion dollars.
suggested_refs: Wheelus Air Base outside Tripoli, evacuated in 1970

stops.name: Cairo, at Nasser's side
stops.date_confidence: the visits run 1969-1970 and are not individually dated in the pool; the stop is pinned to the date of Nasser's death.
stops.campa: He travels repeatedly to Cairo to sit with Gamal Abdel Nasser, the man whose speeches he had organized a schoolyard around in Sabha, and presses union schemes on a president who has already lost one union and receives them carefully. Nasser dies of a heart attack in September 1970. The colonel loses the only living authority he has ever accepted above himself, and spends the next forty-one years addressing the Arab world in a voice with no elder left in it.
suggested_refs: The Arab League summitry of 1969-1970 in Cairo, where the young colonel was introduced to Arab heads of state

stops.name: Damascus, the Federation of Arab Republics
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the Damascus negotiations to 1971 and the proclamation to 1972; 17 April 1971 is the standard signature date of the federation agreement and is not separately verified here.
stops.campa: He negotiates toward a union of Libya, Egypt and Syria, proclaimed as the Federation of Arab Republics and never a working state for a single day: no shared treasury, no shared army, no shared law. Sadat's separate road to Israel will bury it. In September 1971 he resigns his own posts in frustration at the pace of things and is back within the month. Pan-Arabism keeps refusing to become a country. Three decades on he turns the same appetite south, toward Africa.
suggested_refs: The Federation of Arab Republics, proclaimed 1972, dissolved without ever functioning
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

segments.name: The Green Book and the State of the Masses

stops.name: Sinai, Flight 114
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 February 1973. The pool's chronology entry carried the year only and added a targeting claim that the dedicated source does not support; the corrected date and framing are used here.
stops.campa: A Libyan Arab Airlines aircraft on the Tripoli to Cairo run strays off course in bad weather with failed instruments and crosses out of Egyptian airspace into Israeli-held Sinai. Israeli fighters shoot it down. One hundred and eight people die, among them Salah Busir, a former Libyan foreign minister. Tripoli's recrimination falls as much on Cairo for failing to protect the flight as on Israel for firing. The Jihad Fund he set up in 1970 to pay for armed groups fighting Israel is by then three years old.
suggested_refs: Libyan Arab Airlines Flight 114, shot down over the Sinai on 21 February 1973

stops.name: Zuwarah, the Popular Revolution
stops.date_confidence: the research pool contradicts itself: the chronology gives 16 April 1973 and the geography gives 15 April. 16 April is taken here and the contradiction is left unresolved.
stops.campa: In the coastal town of Zuwarah he announces a five-point plan: suspension of the existing laws, purge of the politically sick, arming of the people, an administrative revolution, and a cultural revolution against imported ideas. General People's Committees are to be formed everywhere, in factories, in schools, in ministries. Books judged deviant are burned in public. The state begins dissolving itself on paper while the council that ordered the dissolution keeps every weapon it holds.
stops.quote: The democratic press is that which is issued by a People's Committee, comprising all the groups of society.
stops.quote_source: The Green Book, Part One, chapter on the Press (1975), verified against the Internet Archive scan, item 'gaddafi-green-book'
suggested_refs: The Zuwarah speech of April 1973, founding text of the General People's Committees
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya

stops.name: Tripoli, the oil taken
stops.date_confidence: September 1973 attested for the fifty-one percent nationalization; day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. The BP expropriation at Sarir is attested to December 1971.
stops.campa: British Petroleum's share of the Sarir field was expropriated in December 1971. In September 1973 the government nationalizes fifty-one percent of every foreign producer operating in the country, and that autumn the price of crude quadruples. An oil state of two million people acquires the revenue of a middle power, and a man who answers to no parliament acquires the spending of it: subsidies, literacy campaigns, water schemes, Soviet arms, and the funding of movements on four continents.
stops.quote: Nothing would please me more, but who else would pump the oil that we need?
stops.quote_source: Time magazine interview, 2 April 1973, asked whether he would expel the Americans from Libya
suggested_refs: The Sarir field and the 1973 nationalization decrees

stops.name: Tripoli, Part One of the Green Book
stops.date_confidence: Part One late 1975, Part Two early 1977, Part Three September 1981; the pool's chronology entry wrongly compressed all three into 1975, and the main Wikipedia article's '1975 and 1979' conflicts with the dedicated article. Month within late 1975 not fixed, defaulted.
stops.campa: Part One appears, The Solution of the Problem of Democracy, a slim volume in green covers arguing that representation is a fraud and that the only democracy is direct rule through people's congresses. Part Two on the economy follows in 1977 and Part Three on the social basis in 1981. Schoolchildren will study it two hours a week, extracts will be read daily on state radio and television, and it will reach forty-two languages. In March 1976 members of his own council are executed for plotting against him.
stops.quote: A parliament is originally founded to represent the people, but this in itself is undemocratic as democracy means the authority of the people and not an authority acting on their behalf.
stops.quote_source: The Green Book, Part One, 'The Solution of the Problem of Democracy' (1975), verified against the Internet Archive scan, item 'gaddafi-green-book'
suggested_refs: The Green Book in three parts, 1975-1981, and the 1976 English edition of Martin, Brian and O'Keeffe, London

stops.name: Bab al-Azizia, the tent inside the walls
stops.date_confidence: the Jamahiriya declaration is attested to 2 March 1977; the compound is his seat from the 1970s to 2011, so the pin carries a period rather than a single day.
stops.campa: On the second of March the country is renamed the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, the state of the masses, governed in name through people's congresses and in fact from a fortified compound in southern Tripoli. Inside its walls he pitches a Bedouin tent and receives heads of state in it. He holds no office at all. His title is Brother Leader and Guide of the Revolution, which no constitution defines and no term of years limits, and he keeps it until he is killed.
stops.quote: Plebiscites are a fraud against democracy. Those who vote "yes" or "no" do not, in fact, express their free will but, rather, are silenced by the modern conception of democracy as they are not allowed to say more than "yes" or "no".
stops.quote_source: The Green Book, Part One (1975), verified against the Internet Archive scan, item 'gaddafi-green-book'
suggested_refs: The Bab al-Azizia compound in southern Tripoli, seat of a man who held no office
sources: Reuters and Al Jazeera reporting on Bab al-Azizia, 2011

segments.name: The Jihad Fund and the Long Reach

stops.name: Munich, the Olympic village
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Jihad Fund, established in 1970 to finance armed groups fighting Israel, pays for the Black September Organization. Its men enter the Olympic village before dawn and take the Israeli team hostage; the night ends at a military airfield outside the city with eleven Israeli athletes and coaches dead. The fund is two years old. What the sources place in Tripoli's hands is the money, not the planning, and Libya is named in the reporting from the first morning.
suggested_refs: The Munich Olympic village and Fürstenfeldbruck airfield, 5-6 September 1972

stops.name: Aouzou, the strip annexed
stops.date_confidence: 1973 attested for the occupation and annexation; month not fixed in the sources reached, defaulted. The pool's coordinate was some sixty kilometres too far south and is corrected to the oasis of Aouzou itself.
stops.campa: Libyan forces occupy the band of northern Chad along the border and the government annexes it, resting the claim on an unratified Franco-Italian accord and on the mineral wealth reported under the sand. The occupation holds twenty-one years. In February 1994 the International Court of Justice rules for Chad by sixteen votes to one and the Libyan withdrawal is complete by June. It is the only territory he ever annexes, and the court takes it back from him without a shot fired.
suggested_refs: The ICJ judgment, Territorial Dispute (Libya/Chad), February 1994

stops.name: Tripoli, the Argentine minister's errand
stops.date_confidence: 1974 attested; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01 January, byte-identical with the pin already carried in jose_lopez_rega.journey.json and inherited by licio_gelli.journey.json.
stops.campa: José López Rega, Isabel Perón's minister of social welfare and founder of the Triple A death squads, arrives in the capital representing the Argentine government. No agenda, no interlocutor and no result is recorded in any reachable source; only that he came. Licio Gelli, grandmaster of the Propaganda Due lodge, is placed by later and unverified accounts at the centre of an oil and arms triangle joining Tripoli, Rome and Buenos Aires, and his own file inherits this pin unchanged.
suggested_refs: The 1974 Argentine mission to Tripoli, recorded in jose_lopez_rega.journey.json and licio_gelli.journey.json without agenda or result

stops.name: Kampala, the alliance with Idi Amin
stops.date_confidence: the alliance runs 1972-1979; pinned to the Libyan deployment during the Tanzanian invasion in early 1979, whose exact dates are not fixed in the pool.
stops.campa: He arms Idi Amin and, when Tanzania invades Uganda, sends Libyan troops to hold Kampala for him. They arrive in a war they cannot read, take heavy losses, and are pulled out; Amin's government falls and he flees the country. The same oil account is paying, across the same decade, liberation movements, insurgencies, and the revolutionary government of Thomas Sankara at Ouagadougou. Uganda is the first African intervention to end with Libyan soldiers dead on foreign ground and the client gone.
suggested_refs: The Libyan expeditionary force in the Uganda-Tanzania War, 1979
sources: BBC News historical coverage of the Uganda-Tanzania War
Press and academic accounts of Sankara-Gaddafi relations

stops.name: Mecca, the circuit of the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not documentation. General biographical accounts have him perform the hajj at least once during the reign; no year is confirmed in any source reached, and 1980 is a placeholder inside the reign rather than an attested date. The pin is the canonical Kaaba coordinate already carried by abdelkader.journey.json.
stops.campa: He performs the hajj at least once during the reign, walking the seven circuits of the Kaaba as one pilgrim among two million, and folds the obligation into the Islamic register of his speeches at home. He also legislates on religion by decree, dating the Muslim calendar from the Prophet's death rather than the hijra, and is denounced from pulpits for it. Emir Abdelkader circled this same stone twice, at seventeen beside his father and at fifty-five as a man Europe had decorated.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, station shared with abdelkader.journey.json
sources: General biographical accounts; specific year not confirmed in available sources

stops.name: N'Djamena, the Toyota War
stops.date_confidence: the Chadian-Libyan conflict runs 1978-1987; pinned to the decisive phase of March 1987, whose day-level dates are not fixed in the pool.
stops.campa: Nine years of Libyan intervention in Chad's civil war end in the desert north, where Chadian fighters mounted on Toyota pickup trucks with recoilless rifles bolted to the beds destroy an armoured force equipped from Moscow. Libya loses aircraft, tanks and thousands of men to an enemy that drives to the battle in commercial vehicles. The war takes its name from the trucks. He holds the Aouzou Strip for seven years more and then loses that too, in a courtroom.
suggested_refs: The Toyota War of 1987, final phase of the Chadian-Libyan conflict
sources: Vandewalle, A History of Modern Libya
Press reporting on the Chadian-Libyan conflict

stops.name: Bab al-Azizia, El Dorado Canyon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 April 1986. The death of the adopted infant daughter is his own claim and was doubted at the time; it remains doubted.
stops.campa: Ten days after a bomb in a West Berlin discotheque used by American servicemen, United States aircraft flying from British bases and from carriers strike Tripoli and Benghazi. His compound is among the targets and he survives it. He states that an adopted infant daughter, Hana, was killed in the raid. Six days before the aircraft came, the American president had described him to the White House press corps without naming him, in an answer to Helen Thomas.
stops.quote: Well, we know that this mad dog of the Middle East has a goal of a world revolution, Moslem fundamentalist revolution, which is targeted on many of his own Arab compatriots.
stops.quote_source: Ronald Reagan, The President's News Conference, 9 April 1986, transcript at the American Presidency Project
suggested_refs: Operation El Dorado Canyon, 15 April 1986, and the bronze fist raised afterwards inside the compound
sources: US Department of Defense records, Operation El Dorado Canyon
American Presidency Project, presidential news conference of 9 April 1986

stops.name: Lockerbie, Flight 103
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A bomb in the forward hold destroys a Pan Am 747 over southern Scotland. Two hundred and fifty-nine people in the aircraft and eleven on the ground are killed, and wreckage falls across the town. On 13 November 1991 Scottish and American prosecutors indict two Libyan intelligence officers, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah, for murder. He refuses to hand them over. In 1992 the Security Council closes the country's airspace and the isolation begins.
suggested_refs: The Lockerbie indictments of 13 November 1991 and UN Security Council sanctions of 1992

stops.name: The Ténéré, Flight 772
stops.date_confidence: September 1989 attested in the pool; the 19 September date and the crash coordinates are the standard published ones and were not re-verified against a live source this session.
stops.campa: Nine months after Lockerbie a French DC-10 flying from Brazzaville to Paris breaks apart over the Ténéré desert of northern Niger and falls in pieces across open sand. French investigators attribute the bomb to Libyan agents. Two airliners are down in nine months, one over a Scottish town and one over open desert, and Libyan agents are named for both. The families wait fourteen years: the compensation for Flight 772 is settled in 2003, the year the government gives up its weapons programmes.
suggested_refs: UTA Flight 772, destroyed over Niger in September 1989

stops.name: Abu Salim, the prison yard
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 June 1996. The toll is Human Rights Watch's estimate of roughly 1,270; the pool's chronology gave 1,200 and is corrected here.
stops.campa: Prisoners in the Tripoli political prison riot over conditions and are promised negotiation. What follows in the yards is reconstructed by Human Rights Watch at roughly one thousand two hundred and seventy dead within a few hours. The state denies it for eight years while families go on delivering food parcels for men already buried. He admits the killings publicly in April 2004. The lawyer who represents those families is arrested in Benghazi in February 2011.
stops.quote: When everyone is part of the people's congress, what need is there for an opposition? Opposition to what? You oppose a government! If there is no government, and the people govern themselves on their own, what are they going to oppose? Something that isn't there?
stops.quote_source: Interview with Oriana Fallaci, Corriere della Sera, 2 December 1979, cited via Wikiquote's sourced entry; the Corriere original was not inspected
suggested_refs: Human Rights Watch, 'Libya: June 1996 Killings at Abu Salim Prison' (2006)

stops.name: Pretoria, Mandela's friend
stops.date_confidence: the relationship is attested across the 1990s without a single fixed date in the pool; the sanction-breaking visit is usually dated October 1997 and was not re-verified this session.
stops.campa: Nelson Mandela, out of prison and president of South Africa, refuses Western demands that he cut Libya off, saying that those who backed the struggle against apartheid when it was unfashionable will not be dropped now that it is won. He flies to Tripoli while the air embargo still stands, takes the criticism from Washington and London, and goes on working at the arrangement that will put the Lockerbie accused before a Scottish court sitting outside Scotland.
suggested_refs: Mandela's public defence of Libya and his mediation toward the Lockerbie trial
sources: Mandela's public statements and press coverage of South Africa-Libya relations, 1990s

stops.name: Camp Zeist, the two men handed over
stops.date_confidence: handover attested to 5 April 1999; trial 3 May 2000 to 31 January 2001. The pool named 'The Hague' and gave a coordinate matching neither city; the pin is corrected to the disused air base near Utrecht.
stops.campa: After seven years of sanctions and mediation the two accused are flown to a disused air base near Utrecht and handed to Scottish police. A Scottish court sits on Dutch soil, under Scots law, without a jury, from May 2000 to January 2001. Megrahi is convicted and Fhimah is acquitted. In 2009 Megrahi is released on medical grounds and flown home to a crowd at Tripoli airport. In 2003 the government accepts responsibility for its officials and pays out more than two billion dollars.
suggested_refs: Kamp van Zeist near Utrecht, where a Scottish court sat on Dutch soil
sources: BBC News coverage of the Lockerbie trial, 2000-2001

segments.name: The King of Kings of Africa

stops.name: Tripoli, the weapons renounced
stops.date_confidence: 2003 attested in the pool; 19 December is the announcement date in the standard accounts and was not separately verified here.
stops.campa: Nine months after Baghdad falls, the government announces that it will dismantle its chemical and nuclear weapons programmes and open the country to inspection. The centrifuges bought on the black market are crated and flown to the United States. Sanctions come off, embassies reopen, the oil majors return, and the man an American president had called a mad dog is received in European capitals as a partner. Eight years later the same capitals send aircraft over the same country.
suggested_refs: The December 2003 disarmament declaration and the removal of Libyan nuclear materials

stops.name: Paris, the tent in the Marigny gardens
stops.date_confidence: December 2007 attested for the five-day visit; the exact opening day is not fixed in the sources reached. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate carried by abdelkader.journey.json rather than the pool's variant.
stops.campa: Invited by President Sarkozy, he arrives for a five-day state visit and pitches his Bedouin tent in the garden of the Hôtel de Marigny beside the Élysée. Ministers protest in public and the contracts are signed anyway; he goes on to Madrid the same season. A hundred and sixty years earlier France shipped Emir Abdelkader into captivity at Toulon, Pau and Amboise on a broken promise and then decorated him. Abdelkader crossed into France under guard. This one crosses by invitation and sleeps in a tent on state ground beside the president's house.
suggested_refs: The gardens of the Hôtel de Marigny, December 2007
sources: BBC and Reuters reporting on the 2007 Paris visit

stops.name: Benghazi, proclaimed King of Kings
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28 August 2008 at Benghazi. The pool's geography lens had conflated this with the African Union chairmanship of February 2009 at Addis Ababa; the two events are separated here.
stops.campa: More than two hundred African traditional kings, chiefs and sultans, brought to Cyrenaica at his expense, proclaim him King of Kings of Africa. He tells them the Arab League has failed him and that Africa is the future, and calls for a single continental state with one army, one passport and one currency. None of the assembled monarchs governs a country, and the title has standing in no legal order anywhere on the continent. He uses it in his own protocol for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The gathering of African traditional rulers at Benghazi, 28 August 2008

stops.name: Benghazi, the treaty with Berlusconi
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 August 2008; the pin is the canonical Benghazi coordinate carried by silvio_berlusconi.journey.json and guido_keller.journey.json.
stops.campa: Two days later Silvio Berlusconi lands in the same city and signs the Treaty of Friendship, Partnership and Cooperation: five billion dollars of Italian investment over twenty years as reparation for the colonial occupation, a formal apology for it, and in exchange Libyan patrols to stop the migrant boats leaving for Lampedusa. In 1911, as that occupation began, Emin Arslan published La Tripolitania from Buenos Aires. The account opened when his grandfather died is settled in cash.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Benghazi, 30 August 2008, between Italy and Libya
sources: Reuters reporting on the 2008 Benghazi treaty

stops.name: Addis Ababa, the African Union chair
stops.date_confidence: elected chairperson 2 February 2009 for a one-year term; attested.
stops.campa: The heads of state elect him chairperson of the African Union for a single year, and he uses the seat to press the United States of Africa he had proclaimed at Benghazi six months earlier. The other governments will not surrender their sovereignty and the plan goes nowhere. He pays a large share of the union's budget and builds mosques, hotels and banks across the continent. He is refused a second term. Two years later this body fails to stop the intervention that ends him.
suggested_refs: The African Union chairmanship, 2009-2010, and the United States of Africa proposal
sources: BBC News, 'Gaddafi elected as AU chairman', February 2009

stops.name: Rome, the tent at Villa Doria Pamphilj
stops.date_confidence: June 2009 attested; the day is not fixed in the source used and is defaulted to 01, as in silvio_berlusconi.journey.json, from which this pin is inherited.
stops.campa: He arrives for the state visit that is the visible half of the Benghazi treaty and pitches the tent in the park of a seventeenth-century Roman villa. On his uniform he wears a photograph of a Libyan resistance leader taken in chains by the Italians, and Berlusconi's government receives him with the photograph in place. Gabriele D'Annunzio wrote the verse that carried Italy into Libya in 1911. The pinned photograph answers it in a Roman garden ninety-eight years later.
suggested_refs: The park of Villa Doria Pamphilj, June 2009, pin inherited from silvio_berlusconi.journey.json
sources: Reuters and BBC reporting on the 2009 Rome visit

stops.name: New York, ninety-six minutes at the General Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In his first appearance at the United Nations he speaks for ninety-six minutes against a fifteen-minute allocation, tears pages from a copy of the Charter, calls the Security Council a terror council, and proposes moving the headquarters out of the United States. His interpreter gives out before he does. He has arrived in the city without lodging: Bedford in New York and Englewood in New Jersey both block the encampment on rented estate ground amid public protest, and he sleeps in Manhattan.
stops.quote: There is no state with a democracy except Libya on the whole planet.
stops.quote_source: Video lecture to students at Columbia University, 23 March 2006, reported by BBC News
suggested_refs: The UN General Assembly address of 23 September 2009, and the blocked encampments at Bedford and Englewood
sources: UN transcript and BBC/Reuters coverage of the 2009 UNGA speech
New York Times and Reuters reporting, September 2009

stops.name: Benghazi, the courthouse
stops.date_confidence: the protests are attested to 15-17 February 2011; pinned to the first day.
stops.campa: The lawyer who represents the families of the Abu Salim dead is arrested, and the relatives gather outside the courthouse on the corniche where they have gathered every week for years. This time the city joins them, and within three days eastern Libya is in open revolt. The transitional council that Western governments will recognize as the government of Libya forms inside this building. Plato lodged near Cyrene in this province and Dihya fought Arab armies across it.
suggested_refs: The Benghazi courthouse on the corniche, seat of the transitional council from February 2011
sources: BBC News timeline of the Libyan uprising, February 2011

stops.name: Luqa, the pilots who would not bomb
stops.date_confidence: reported as 21 February 2011; the date could not be re-verified against a live source this session and the pool flags it as reported but unconfirmed. The pin is Malta International Airport at Luqa, not Valletta city as the pool had it.
stops.campa: Two Libyan air force pilots ordered to bomb the crowds in Benghazi fly their Mirage F1s north across the Mediterranean instead and land at Malta's international airport, asking for asylum. The government's account of a foreign conspiracy is contradicted inside a week by its own aircrew. Ambassadors resign in a dozen capitals. In March NATO begins flying over the country, and the regime that closed the foreign bases in 1970 is bombed from the sea it faces.
suggested_refs: Malta International Airport at Luqa, landing ground of the defecting Mirage F1s
sources: BBC News and Reuters reporting on the Malta pilot defections, February 2011

stops.name: Rixos Hotel, the last briefings
stops.date_confidence: the press operation runs February to August 2011; pinned to the final month, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The government keeps the foreign press corps in one hotel in the capital and briefs it daily on victories while NATO aircraft cross overhead and the map shrinks. When the rebels take Tripoli in late August the journalists are held inside the building for five days by loyalist guards who do not accept that the war is over. The last authority in the country deciding what reporters may see is the authority that wrote in the Green Book what a newspaper is.
stops.quote: A newspaper owned by any individual is his or her own, and expresses only his or her point of view. Any claim that a newspaper represents public opinion is groundless because it actually expresses the viewpoint of that private individual.
stops.quote_source: The Green Book, Part One, chapter on the Press (1975), verified against the Internet Archive scan, item 'gaddafi-green-book'
suggested_refs: The Rixos Al Nasr hotel in Tripoli, press cage of the last six months
sources: BBC and Reuters correspondent reporting from the Rixos, 2011

stops.name: Algiers, the family crosses
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 August 2011.
stops.campa: Six days after the fall of the capital his wife Safia, his daughter Aisha and his sons Hannibal and Mohammed cross the western border into Algeria and are granted refuge. His son Saadi goes south instead and is taken in at Niamey in Niger despite an international arrest warrant, which the new authorities in Tripoli protest. Part of the family will move on again, to Oman, on terms and dates that no reachable source sets out. He does not leave the country.
suggested_refs: The Algerian and Nigerien refuges of the Gaddafi family, August and September 2011
sources: BBC News, 'Gaddafi family flees to Algeria', 29 August 2011
BBC News reporting on Saadi Gaddafi's flight to Niger, September 2011
Later press reporting on the dispersal of the family; terms not documented

stops.name: Bani Walid, the last refuge
stops.date_confidence: the loyalist retreat to Bani Walid is attested to August-September 2011; the day is not fixed and is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The loyalist towns of the interior hold out after the capital falls, and he moves among them with a shrinking convoy, sending audio messages to stations that no longer broadcast from any ground he controls. In April he had written to the American president in his own English, addressing him as a son, asking him to call the aircraft off, and signing the letter from a Tripoli he still held. It was carried in full by American newspapers and changed nothing in the flying schedule.
stops.quote: democracy and building of civil society cannot be achieved by means of missiles and aircraft, or by backing armed member of AlQuaeda in Benghazi.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Barack Obama, signed Tripoli 5 April 2011 and reported 6 April; full text published by CBS News and the Kennebec Journal. Spelling and capitalization are as printed.
suggested_refs: Bani Walid, one of the last loyalist towns of the interior
sources: Reuters and Al Jazeera reporting on the fall of Tripoli, 2011
CBS News, 'Full text of Qaddafi's recent letter to Obama'

stops.name: Sirte, the culvert
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He returns to the district he was born in, besieged and starving, and on the twentieth of October a convoy leaving the town at first light is struck from the air. He takes cover in a concrete drainage culvert under the road with a handful of guards. Fighters from Misrata pull him out alive, and he is beaten, paraded and killed within the hour, filmed throughout on telephones. He dies about eight kilometres from the tent he was born in, aged sixty-eight or sixty-nine.
stops.quote: We came, we saw, he died.
stops.quote_source: Hillary Clinton, on-camera remark to CBS News on being told of Gaddafi's death, 20 October 2011
suggested_refs: The drainage culvert on the western road out of Sirte
sources: BBC News, 'Gaddafi killed as Sirte falls', 20 October 2011
NATO statement on the convoy strike

segments.name: The Freezer and the Unmarked Grave

stops.name: Misrata, the body in the freezer
stops.date_confidence: the public viewing is attested to 21-24 October 2011; pinned to the first day.
stops.campa: The body is driven to the coastal town where he finished secondary school half a century earlier and laid in a commercial cold store. For four days the public files past it in queues, families waiting their turn, some having driven hundreds of kilometres across the country to look at it and be certain. The transitional council's oil minister explains that it is being kept so that everybody knows he is dead. His son Mutassim is laid beside him. On the twenty-fourth the doors are closed.
suggested_refs: The commercial cold store at Misrata, 21-24 October 2011

stops.name: The Libyan Desert, buried before dawn
stops.date_confidence: the burial was announced on 25 October 2011 and is attested. The coordinate is an approximation of the desert interior south of Sirte and is not a claim about the site, which has never been disclosed. That the grave remains unlocated is widely repeated and was not re-verified against a primary source this session.
stops.campa: Before first light he is buried in an unmarked grave at a place the transitional council will not name, together with Mutassim and the former defence chief Abu Bakr Younis Jabr. The information minister cites a religious ruling that the place must stay unknown, so that it cannot become a shrine or a rallying ground. An amateur video records the funeral prayers. Rumours that he survived, that the man on the film was a double, circulate from that month onward and have not stopped.
suggested_refs: The undisclosed desert grave of 25 October 2011, never located
sources: widely repeated contemporary reporting; the survival rumours are tradition, not confirmed reporting

stops.name: Bab al-Azizia, the Friday market in the ruins
stops.date_confidence: compound captured 23 August 2011, demolition begun 17 October 2011, the market and the rubble described as of February 2012; day within that month not fixed, defaulted.
stops.campa: The compound was overrun on the twenty-third of August 2011 and its statues broken, among them the bronze fist crushing an American fighter jet raised after the 1986 raid. Bulldozers started on the outer walls in October and stopped short of levelling the site. By that winter Tripoli's Friday market had moved inside the walls and families were living in the rubble. A plan to finish the demolition and lay out a public park was announced and never carried out.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Bab al-Azizia, market ground and squat from 2012

stops.name: Sabha, the son registers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 November 2021; candidacy rejected 16 November and reinstated by a court on 2 December 2021.
stops.campa: Saif al-Islam, captured in the desert in November 2011, sentenced to death in absentia by a Tripoli court in 2015 and released by his Zintani captors in 2017, appears in public for the first time in seven years to register as a candidate for president. He does it in the Fezzan oasis town from which his father was expelled as a schoolboy for making a speech. The commission rejects the papers two days later, a court reinstates them in December, and the election is never held.
stops.quote: You need to come back slowly, slowly. Like a striptease.
stops.quote_source: Saif al-Islam Gaddafi on his re-emergence, 14 November 2021, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Saif al-Islam Gaddafi'
suggested_refs: The electoral registration office at Sabha, 14 November 2021

stops.name: Zintan, the second grave
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 February 2026; burial at Bani Walid on 6 February 2026.
stops.campa: Four gunmen enter a house in the mountain town where the militia that captured him had held him prisoner and then, after 2017, sheltered him. They kill him in it. He is buried three days later at Bani Walid, one of the towns that held out for his father through the autumn of 2011. Fifteen years after the culvert the family has a marked grave in Libyan ground, and the man who governed the country for forty-two years without holding an office in it does not.
suggested_refs: The Bani Walid burial of 6 February 2026, the family's first marked grave in Libya since 2011
